## What we will explore

In the previous chapter, we fitted one model and obtained one set of optimized parameters. We will now ask:

- Would the parameters change if we fitted a different subset of the observations?
- How well does each model predict observations that were not used for fitting?
- Where are the spatial parameter estimates stable, and where are they uncertain?

We will move through the ideas in a simple order:

**one train/test split → k-fold cross-validation → repeated cross-validation → ensembles → parameter and prediction ranges → spatial uncertainty maps**

::: {.callout-tip title="The key change in perspective"}
The previous chapter asked, **“What is the best fitted model?”**
This chapter asks, **“How much does the fitted answer change?”**
:::

## Setup and short recap

Install the packages once if needed.

```{r}
#| eval: false
install.packages(c("readr", "nls2", "pso", "randomForest", "terra", "spData"))
```

Load the packages.

```{r}
library(readr)
library(nls2)
library(pso)
library(randomForest)
```

Set the validation choices.

```{r}
#| label: settings

min_drydown_steps <- 5
k_folds <- 5
n_repeats <- 10
analysis_seed <- 100
```

### Read the simplified data

```{r}
#| label: download-site-data

csv_url <- paste0(
  "https://github.com/Vinit-Sehgal/AGRO4092/raw/refs/heads/main/",
  "SampleData-master/US-TON_SM-EF.csv"
)

download.file(
  csv_url,
  destfile = "US-TON_SM-EF.csv",
  mode = "wb"
)
```

```{r}
#| label: read-site-data
#| warning: false

eddy_data <- read_csv(
  "US-TON_SM-EF.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

eddy_data$date <- as.Date(eddy_data$date)
eddy_data <- eddy_data[order(eddy_data$date), ]
```

### Recreate the drydown data

```{r}
#| label: drydown-data

eddy_data$SM_change <- c(NA_real_, diff(eddy_data$SM))
eddy_data$is_drydown <-
  is.finite(eddy_data$SM_change) & eddy_data$SM_change <= 0

eddy_data$drydown_id <- cumsum(!eddy_data$is_drydown)
eddy_data$drydown_length <- ave(
  eddy_data$is_drydown,
  eddy_data$drydown_id,
  FUN = sum
)

drydown_data <- subset(
  eddy_data,
  is_drydown &
    drydown_length >= min_drydown_steps &
    is.finite(SM) &
    is.finite(EF)
)

drydown_data$observation_id <- seq_len(nrow(drydown_data))

cat("Observations:", nrow(drydown_data), "\n")
cat("Drydown events:", length(unique(drydown_data$drydown_id)), "\n")
```

::: {.callout-important title="Keep complete drydowns together"}
Neighboring observations from one drydown are not independent.
We will assign whole drydown events—not individual rows—to training or validation groups.
This reduces information leakage.
:::

### Reuse the physical model and fitting functions

The chapter is self-contained, so we repeat compact versions of the functions from the previous chapter.
The revised optimization bounds remain unchanged.

```{r}
#| label: model-functions

piecewise_EF <- function(SM, theta_d, theta_w, EF_max) {
  ifelse(
    SM <= theta_d,
    0,
    ifelse(
      SM >= theta_w,
      EF_max,
      EF_max * (SM - theta_d) / (theta_w - theta_d)
    )
  )
}

model_error <- function(parameters, SM, EF) {
  predicted <- piecewise_EF(
    SM,
    parameters[1],
    parameters[2],
    parameters[3]
  )

  mean((EF - predicted)^2, na.rm = TRUE)
}
```

```{r}
#| label: nls-fitting-function

fit_NLS <- function(SM, EF) {
  keep <- is.finite(SM) & is.finite(EF)
  SM <- SM[keep]
  EF <- EF[keep]

  empty_result <- c(
    theta_d = NA_real_,
    theta_w = NA_real_,
    EF_max = NA_real_
  )

  if (length(SM) < 10 || length(unique(SM)) < 4) {
    return(empty_result)
  }

  lower <- c(
    theta_d = 0.02,
    theta_w = unname(quantile(SM, 0.35)),
    EF_max = 0.20
  )

  upper <- c(
    theta_d = unname(quantile(SM, 0.30)),
    theta_w = unname(quantile(SM, 0.98)),
    EF_max = 1.00
  )

  if (any(!is.finite(c(lower, upper))) || any(lower >= upper)) {
    return(empty_result)
  }

  model_data <- data.frame(SM = SM, EF = EF)

  search_grid <- expand.grid(
    theta_d = seq(lower["theta_d"], upper["theta_d"], length.out = 6),
    theta_w = seq(lower["theta_w"], upper["theta_w"], length.out = 6),
    EF_max = seq(lower["EF_max"], upper["EF_max"], length.out = 6)
  )

  start_fit <- nls2(
    EF ~ piecewise_EF(SM, theta_d, theta_w, EF_max),
    data = model_data,
    start = search_grid,
    algorithm = "brute-force"
  )

  fit <- nls(
    EF ~ piecewise_EF(SM, theta_d, theta_w, EF_max),
    data = model_data,
    start = as.list(coef(start_fit)),
    algorithm = "port",
    lower = lower,
    upper = upper,
    control = nls.control(maxiter = 200, warnOnly = TRUE)
  )

  parameters <- coef(fit)[c("theta_d", "theta_w", "EF_max")]
  setNames(as.numeric(parameters), names(empty_result))
}
```

```{r}
#| label: pso-fitting-function

fit_PSO <- function(SM, EF) {
  keep <- is.finite(SM) & is.finite(EF)
  SM <- SM[keep]
  EF <- EF[keep]

  empty_result <- c(
    theta_d = NA_real_,
    theta_w = NA_real_,
    EF_max = NA_real_
  )

  if (length(SM) < 10 || length(unique(SM)) < 4) {
    return(empty_result)
  }

  lower <- c(
    theta_d = 0.02,
    theta_w = unname(quantile(SM, 0.35)),
    EF_max = 0.20
  )

  upper <- c(
    theta_d = unname(quantile(SM, 0.30)),
    theta_w = unname(quantile(SM, 0.98)),
    EF_max = 1.00
  )

  if (any(!is.finite(c(lower, upper))) || any(lower >= upper)) {
    return(empty_result)
  }

  fit <- psoptim(
    par = (lower + upper) / 2,
    fn = model_error,
    SM = SM,
    EF = EF,
    lower = lower,
    upper = upper,
    control = list(
      s = 30,
      maxit = 60,
      trace = 0
    )
  )

  setNames(as.numeric(fit$par), names(empty_result))
}
```

Define the statistics that we will use.

```{r}
#| label: validation-statistics

validation_stats <- function(observed, predicted) {
  keep <- complete.cases(observed, predicted)
  observed <- observed[keep]
  predicted <- predicted[keep]

  rmse <- sqrt(mean((observed - predicted)^2))
  mae <- mean(abs(observed - predicted))
  bias <- mean(predicted - observed)

  if (length(observed) > 2 &&
      sd(observed) > 0 &&
      sd(predicted) > 0) {
    r2 <- cor(observed, predicted)^2
  } else {
    r2 <- NA_real_
  }

  data.frame(
    RMSE = rmse,
    MAE = mae,
    Bias = bias,
    R2 = r2
  )
}
```

- **RMSE** gives more weight to large errors.
- **MAE** is the average absolute error.
- **Bias** is predicted minus observed EF.
- **$R^2$** describes association, but it does not measure agreement by itself.

## Begin with one train/test split

A model should be evaluated using observations that were not used to fit it.
We will use 80% of the drydown events for training and 20% for testing.

```{r}
#| label: train-test-split

set.seed(analysis_seed)

event_ids <- unique(drydown_data$drydown_id)
train_ids <- sample(
  event_ids,
  size = floor(0.80 * length(event_ids))
)

train_data <- subset(drydown_data, drydown_id %in% train_ids)
test_data <- subset(drydown_data, !drydown_id %in% train_ids)

cat("Training events:", length(unique(train_data$drydown_id)), "\n")
cat("Testing events:", length(unique(test_data$drydown_id)), "\n")
```

Fit the two physical models to the training events.
`tryCatch()` prevents one failed fit from ending the comparison.

```{r}
#| label: train-piecewise-models

empty_parameters <- c(
  theta_d = NA_real_,
  theta_w = NA_real_,
  EF_max = NA_real_
)

nls_train_parameters <- tryCatch(
  fit_NLS(train_data$SM, train_data$EF),
  error = function(e) empty_parameters
)

set.seed(analysis_seed)

pso_train_parameters <- tryCatch(
  fit_PSO(train_data$SM, train_data$EF),
  error = function(e) empty_parameters
)
```

Predict the withheld test events.

```{r}
#| label: predict-test-piecewise

nls_test_prediction <- piecewise_EF(
  test_data$SM,
  nls_train_parameters["theta_d"],
  nls_train_parameters["theta_w"],
  nls_train_parameters["EF_max"]
)

pso_test_prediction <- piecewise_EF(
  test_data$SM,
  pso_train_parameters["theta_d"],
  pso_train_parameters["theta_w"],
  pso_train_parameters["EF_max"]
)
```

Fit and predict with Random Forest using the same split.

```{r}
#| label: train-test-random-forest

set.seed(analysis_seed)

rf_train_fit <- randomForest(
  EF ~ SM,
  data = train_data,
  ntree = 500,
  mtry = 1,
  nodesize = 10
)

rf_test_prediction <- predict(
  rf_train_fit,
  newdata = test_data
)
```

Compare the test statistics.

```{r}
#| label: one-split-statistics

one_split_results <- rbind(
  NLS2 = validation_stats(test_data$EF, nls_test_prediction),
  PSO = validation_stats(test_data$EF, pso_test_prediction),
  `Random Forest` = validation_stats(test_data$EF, rf_test_prediction)
)

one_split_results
```

::: {.callout-important title="Training error is not validation error"}
A model can fit its training observations closely and still predict new observations poorly.
Model comparison should therefore use withheld predictions, not only the data used during fitting.
:::

## Move from one split to k-fold cross-validation

One split depends on which events happened to enter the test group.
In **k-fold cross-validation**, we divide the events into $k$ folds, fit on $k-1$ folds, and validate on the remaining fold.
Every fold takes a turn as validation data.

### Create event-level folds

```{r}
#| label: make-folds

make_folds <- function(data, k = 5, seed = 100) {
  set.seed(seed)

  events <- sample(unique(data$drydown_id))

  fold_table <- data.frame(
    drydown_id = events,
    fold = rep(seq_len(k), length.out = length(events))
  )

  merge(
    data,
    fold_table,
    by = "drydown_id",
    all.x = TRUE,
    sort = FALSE
  )
}
```

Inspect one assignment.

```{r}
#| label: inspect-folds

example_folds <- make_folds(
  drydown_data,
  k = k_folds,
  seed = analysis_seed
)

table(example_folds$fold)
```

### Repeat the k-fold process

Repeated cross-validation reshuffles the fold assignment and runs the complete k-fold process again.
With 5 folds and 10 repeats, each method can produce as many as 50 fitted models.
Those fitted models form an **ensemble**.

## Cross-validate NLS2/NLS and PSO

The shared function below calls either `fit_NLS()` or `fit_PSO()`.
It stores the fitted parameters, validation statistics, and withheld predictions.

```{r}
#| label: piecewise-cross-validation

cross_validate_piecewise <- function(
    data,
    fit_function,
    method,
    k = 5,
    repeats = 10,
    seed = 100) {

  parameters <- data.frame()
  statistics <- data.frame()
  predictions <- data.frame()

  for (repeat_id in seq_len(repeats)) {
    cv_data <- make_folds(
      data,
      k = k,
      seed = seed + repeat_id
    )

    for (fold_id in seq_len(k)) {
      train <- subset(cv_data, fold != fold_id)
      test <- subset(cv_data, fold == fold_id)

      set.seed(seed + 1000 * repeat_id + fold_id)

      pars <- tryCatch(
        fit_function(train$SM, train$EF),
        error = function(e) c(
          theta_d = NA_real_,
          theta_w = NA_real_,
          EF_max = NA_real_
        )
      )

      if (length(pars) != 3 || any(!is.finite(pars))) {
        next
      }

      predicted <- piecewise_EF(
        test$SM,
        pars["theta_d"],
        pars["theta_w"],
        pars["EF_max"]
      )

      parameters <- rbind(
        parameters,
        data.frame(
          repeat_id = repeat_id,
          fold_id = fold_id,
          method = method,
          theta_d = unname(pars["theta_d"]),
          theta_w = unname(pars["theta_w"]),
          EF_max = unname(pars["EF_max"])
        )
      )

      fold_stats <- validation_stats(test$EF, predicted)
      fold_stats$repeat_id <- repeat_id
      fold_stats$fold_id <- fold_id
      fold_stats$method <- method
      statistics <- rbind(statistics, fold_stats)

      predictions <- rbind(
        predictions,
        data.frame(
          repeat_id = repeat_id,
          fold_id = fold_id,
          method = method,
          observation_id = test$observation_id,
          SM = test$SM,
          EF_observed = test$EF,
          EF_predicted = predicted
        )
      )
    }
  }

  list(
    parameters = parameters,
    statistics = statistics,
    predictions = predictions
  )
}
```

::: {.callout-caution title="Do not let tryCatch hide model problems"}
`tryCatch()` is appropriate when many folds are fitted, but it can hide why a fit failed.
While developing the function, run a selected training fold without `tryCatch()` so that R shows the full error.
:::

Run the two physics-based methods with the same fold seeds.

```{r}
#| label: run-piecewise-cross-validation

nls_results <- cross_validate_piecewise(
  drydown_data,
  fit_function = fit_NLS,
  method = "NLS2",
  k = k_folds,
  repeats = n_repeats,
  seed = analysis_seed
)

pso_results <- cross_validate_piecewise(
  drydown_data,
  fit_function = fit_PSO,
  method = "PSO",
  k = k_folds,
  repeats = n_repeats,
  seed = analysis_seed
)
```

Extract the three result types.

```{r}
#| label: extract-piecewise-results

nls_parameters <- nls_results$parameters
pso_parameters <- pso_results$parameters

piecewise_parameters <- rbind(
  nls_parameters,
  pso_parameters
)

piecewise_statistics <- rbind(
  nls_results$statistics,
  pso_results$statistics
)

piecewise_predictions <- rbind(
  nls_results$predictions,
  pso_results$predictions
)
```

## Cross-validate Random Forest

Random Forest does not return the three physical parameters.
We will store its validation statistics, withheld predictions, and fitted forest models.

```{r}
#| label: random-forest-cross-validation

rf_statistics <- data.frame()
rf_predictions <- data.frame()
rf_models <- list()

for (repeat_id in seq_len(n_repeats)) {
  cv_data <- make_folds(
    drydown_data,
    k = k_folds,
    seed = analysis_seed + repeat_id
  )

  for (fold_id in seq_len(k_folds)) {
    train <- subset(cv_data, fold != fold_id)
    test <- subset(cv_data, fold == fold_id)

    fit <- tryCatch(
      {
        set.seed(analysis_seed + 1000 * repeat_id + fold_id)
        randomForest(
          EF ~ SM,
          data = train,
          ntree = 500,
          mtry = 1,
          nodesize = 10
        )
      },
      error = function(e) NULL
    )

    if (is.null(fit)) {
      next
    }

    predicted <- predict(fit, newdata = test)

    fold_stats <- validation_stats(test$EF, predicted)
    fold_stats$repeat_id <- repeat_id
    fold_stats$fold_id <- fold_id
    fold_stats$method <- "Random Forest"
    rf_statistics <- rbind(rf_statistics, fold_stats)

    rf_predictions <- rbind(
      rf_predictions,
      data.frame(
        repeat_id = repeat_id,
        fold_id = fold_id,
        method = "Random Forest",
        observation_id = test$observation_id,
        SM = test$SM,
        EF_observed = test$EF,
        EF_predicted = as.numeric(predicted)
      )
    )

    rf_models[[length(rf_models) + 1]] <- fit
  }
}
```

## Compare out-of-sample performance

Combine the fold statistics and calculate the median for each method.

```{r}
#| label: compare-validation

all_statistics <- rbind(
  piecewise_statistics,
  rf_statistics
)

validation_summary <- aggregate(
  cbind(RMSE, MAE, Bias, R2) ~ method,
  data = all_statistics,
  FUN = median,
  na.rm = TRUE
)

validation_summary
```

Use lower RMSE and MAE, bias near zero, and larger $R^2$ together.
No one statistic tells the complete story.

## Examine parameter uncertainty

The repeated fits give many estimates of each physical parameter.
The spread shows sensitivity to the selected training drydowns.

```{r}
#| label: parameter-boxplots
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4

old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(5, 4.5, 3, 1))

boxplot(
  theta_d ~ method,
  data = piecewise_parameters,
  col = c("salmon", "turquoise3"),
  xlab = "",
  ylab = expression(theta[d]),
  main = "Dry threshold"
)

boxplot(
  theta_w ~ method,
  data = piecewise_parameters,
  col = c("salmon", "turquoise3"),
  xlab = "",
  ylab = expression(theta[w]),
  main = "Wet threshold"
)

boxplot(
  EF_max ~ method,
  data = piecewise_parameters,
  col = c("salmon", "turquoise3"),
  xlab = "",
  ylab = expression(EF[max]),
  main = "Wet plateau"
)

par(old_par)
```

Calculate the median and the 2.5th–97.5th percentile range.

```{r}
#| label: parameter-ranges

parameter_range <- function(x) {
  c(
    median = median(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    lower = quantile(x, 0.025, na.rm = TRUE, names = FALSE),
    upper = quantile(x, 0.975, na.rm = TRUE, names = FALSE)
  )
}

by(
  piecewise_parameters[c("theta_d", "theta_w", "EF_max")],
  piecewise_parameters$method,
  function(x) sapply(x, parameter_range)
)
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Watch for estimates at the bounds"}
A narrow ensemble is not automatically trustworthy.
If many estimates collect at a lower or upper bound, the data may not constrain that parameter, or the chosen search space may be too narrow.
:::

## Examine prediction uncertainty

We will predict EF over the same SM grid with every fitted model.
At each SM value, we will calculate the median prediction and the 2.5th–97.5th percentile ensemble range.

```{r}
#| label: prediction-grid

sm_grid <- seq(
  min(drydown_data$SM, na.rm = TRUE),
  max(drydown_data$SM, na.rm = TRUE),
  length.out = 200
)
```

Build one prediction matrix for each method.
Rows represent SM values, and columns represent ensemble members.

```{r}
#| label: piecewise-prediction-matrices

nls_curve_matrix <- matrix(
  NA_real_,
  nrow = length(sm_grid),
  ncol = nrow(nls_parameters)
)

for (i in seq_len(nrow(nls_parameters))) {
  nls_curve_matrix[, i] <- piecewise_EF(
    sm_grid,
    nls_parameters$theta_d[i],
    nls_parameters$theta_w[i],
    nls_parameters$EF_max[i]
  )
}

pso_curve_matrix <- matrix(
  NA_real_,
  nrow = length(sm_grid),
  ncol = nrow(pso_parameters)
)

for (i in seq_len(nrow(pso_parameters))) {
  pso_curve_matrix[, i] <- piecewise_EF(
    sm_grid,
    pso_parameters$theta_d[i],
    pso_parameters$theta_w[i],
    pso_parameters$EF_max[i]
  )
}
```

```{r}
#| label: random-forest-prediction-matrix

rf_curve_matrix <- matrix(
  NA_real_,
  nrow = length(sm_grid),
  ncol = length(rf_models)
)

for (i in seq_along(rf_models)) {
  rf_curve_matrix[, i] <- predict(
    rf_models[[i]],
    newdata = data.frame(SM = sm_grid)
  )
}
```

Summarize any ensemble matrix with one small function.

```{r}
#| label: summarize-prediction-ensemble

summarize_curves <- function(prediction_matrix) {
  data.frame(
    SM = sm_grid,
    EF_median = apply(prediction_matrix, 1, median, na.rm = TRUE),
    EF_lower = apply(
      prediction_matrix,
      1,
      quantile,
      probs = 0.025,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    EF_upper = apply(
      prediction_matrix,
      1,
      quantile,
      probs = 0.975,
      na.rm = TRUE
    )
  )
}

nls_curve_summary <- summarize_curves(nls_curve_matrix)
pso_curve_summary <- summarize_curves(pso_curve_matrix)
rf_curve_summary <- summarize_curves(rf_curve_matrix)
```

Plot the median curves and their ensemble ranges.

```{r}
#| label: plot-uncertainty-bands
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4.5

curve_list <- list(
  NLS2 = nls_curve_summary,
  PSO = pso_curve_summary,
  `Random Forest` = rf_curve_summary
)

curve_colors <- c("salmon", "turquoise3", "forestgreen")
old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 3, 1))

for (i in seq_along(curve_list)) {
  s <- curve_list[[i]]

  plot(
    drydown_data$SM,
    drydown_data$EF,
    pch = 16,
    cex = 0.65,
    cex.axis = 1.1,
    cex.lab = 1.1,
    col = adjustcolor("grey30", alpha.f = 0.25),
    panel.first = graphics::grid(),
    xlab = expression("Soil moisture"~(m^3~m^{-3})),
    ylab = if (i == 1) "Evaporative fraction" else "",
    main = names(curve_list)[i]
  )

  polygon(
    c(s$SM, rev(s$SM)),
    c(s$EF_lower, rev(s$EF_upper)),
    col = adjustcolor(curve_colors[i], alpha.f = 0.20),
    border = NA
  )

  lines(
    s$SM,
    s$EF_median,
    col = curve_colors[i],
    lwd = 3
  )
}

par(old_par)
```

::: {.callout-note title="The ribbon is an ensemble range"}
The 2.5th–97.5th percentile ribbon describes variation among repeat-fold model fits.
It is not a formal confidence interval and does not include every source of measurement, parameter, and model-structure uncertainty.
:::

## Summarize withheld predictions by observation

Each observation is withheld once per repeat.
Take the median of its repeated out-of-sample predictions.

```{r}
#| label: observation-predictions

all_predictions <- rbind(
  piecewise_predictions,
  rf_predictions
)

observation_predictions <- aggregate(
  EF_predicted ~ observation_id + SM + EF_observed + method,
  data = all_predictions,
  FUN = median,
  na.rm = TRUE
)
```

Plot observed and withheld predictions.

```{r}
#| label: plot-observed-predicted
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4.5

method_names <- c("NLS2", "PSO", "Random Forest")
plot_limits <- range(
  c(
    observation_predictions$EF_observed,
    observation_predictions$EF_predicted
  ),
  na.rm = TRUE
)

old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 3, 1))

for (i in seq_along(method_names)) {
  plot_data <- subset(
    observation_predictions,
    method == method_names[i]
  )

  plot(
    plot_data$EF_observed,
    plot_data$EF_predicted,
    pch = 16,
    cex = 0.65,
    cex.axis = 1.1,
    cex.lab = 1.1,
    col = adjustcolor("grey30", alpha.f = 0.30),
    panel.first = graphics::grid(),
    xlim = plot_limits,
    ylim = plot_limits,
    asp = 1,
    xlab = "Observed EF",
    ylab = if (i == 1) "Median predicted EF" else "",
    main = method_names[i]
  )

  abline(0, 1, lty = 2, lwd = 2)
}

par(old_par)
```

## Map spatial parameter uncertainty

The previous chapter produced one optimized parameter value per raster cell.
We will now repeatedly fit resampled observations within each cell and summarize the resulting parameter distribution.

To keep the demonstration manageable, we will use **PSO only**.
The same idea can be applied to NLS2/NLS.

### Read the matched raster time series

```{r}
#| label: spatial-packages

library(terra)
library(spData)
```

```{r}
#| label: download-spatial-data

download.file(
  "https://github.com/Vinit-Sehgal/AGRO4092/raw/refs/heads/main/SampleData-master/SM.nc",
  destfile = "SM.nc",
  mode = "wb"
)

download.file(
  "https://github.com/Vinit-Sehgal/AGRO4092/raw/refs/heads/main/SampleData-master/EF.nc",
  destfile = "EF.nc",
  mode = "wb"
)

SM <- rast("SM.nc")
EF <- rast("EF.nc")
```

Check that the raster stacks can be paired.

```{r}
#| label: check-spatial-inputs

stopifnot(compareGeom(SM, EF, stopOnError = FALSE))
stopifnot(nlyr(SM) == nlyr(EF))
```

### Test uncertainty for one cell

Choose one well-observed cell.

```{r}
#| label: choose-spatial-cell

complete_count <- xapp(
  SM,
  EF,
  fun = function(SM, EF) sum(is.finite(SM) & is.finite(EF))
)

cell_id <- which.max(values(complete_count, mat = FALSE))
cell_SM <- as.numeric(extract(SM, cell_id, raw = TRUE))
cell_EF <- as.numeric(extract(EF, cell_id, raw = TRUE))
```

Fit repeated 80% subsamples.

```{r}
#| label: one-cell-resampling

n_spatial_samples <- 20
sample_fraction <- 0.80

keep <- is.finite(cell_SM) & is.finite(cell_EF)
cell_SM <- cell_SM[keep]
cell_EF <- cell_EF[keep]

cell_parameters <- matrix(
  NA_real_,
  nrow = n_spatial_samples,
  ncol = 3,
  dimnames = list(
    NULL,
    c("theta_d", "theta_w", "EF_max")
  )
)

set.seed(analysis_seed)

for (i in seq_len(n_spatial_samples)) {
  sample_id <- sample(
    seq_along(cell_SM),
    size = floor(sample_fraction * length(cell_SM)),
    replace = FALSE
  )

  cell_parameters[i, ] <- tryCatch(
    fit_PSO(cell_SM[sample_id], cell_EF[sample_id]),
    error = function(e) c(
      theta_d = NA_real_,
      theta_w = NA_real_,
      EF_max = NA_real_
    )
  )
}

apply(cell_parameters, 2, parameter_range)
```

::: {.callout-important title="What the spatial range means"}
The range answers: **How much does the fitted parameter change when the cell is fitted with different 80% subsets of its matched observations?**
It does not claim that every source of uncertainty has been measured.
:::

### Write a cell function for uncertainty

First define a small summary function.

```{r}
#| label: spatial-parameter-summary

spatial_summary <- function(x) {
  lower <- quantile(x, 0.025, na.rm = TRUE, names = FALSE)
  upper <- quantile(x, 0.975, na.rm = TRUE, names = FALSE)

  c(
    median = median(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    lower = lower,
    upper = upper,
    width = upper - lower
  )
}
```

Now create the function passed to `terra::app()`.
It returns four values for each of the three parameters: median, lower bound, upper bound, and range width.

```{r}
#| label: spatial-uncertainty-function

n_time <- nlyr(SM)
spatial_data <- c(SM, EF)

fit_PSO_uncertainty <- function(x) {
  SM_cell <- x[1:n_time]
  EF_cell <- x[(n_time + 1):(2 * n_time)]

  keep <- is.finite(SM_cell) & is.finite(EF_cell)
  SM_cell <- SM_cell[keep]
  EF_cell <- EF_cell[keep]

  empty_result <- rep(NA_real_, 12)

  if (length(SM_cell) < 20 || length(unique(SM_cell)) < 4) {
    return(empty_result)
  }

  fitted_parameters <- matrix(
    NA_real_,
    nrow = n_spatial_samples,
    ncol = 3
  )

  set.seed(analysis_seed)

  for (i in seq_len(n_spatial_samples)) {
    sample_id <- sample(
      seq_along(SM_cell),
      size = floor(sample_fraction * length(SM_cell)),
      replace = FALSE
    )

    fitted_parameters[i, ] <- tryCatch(
      fit_PSO(SM_cell[sample_id], EF_cell[sample_id]),
      error = function(e) c(
        theta_d = NA_real_,
        theta_w = NA_real_,
        EF_max = NA_real_
      )
    )
  }

  fitted_parameters <- fitted_parameters[
    complete.cases(fitted_parameters),
    ,
    drop = FALSE
  ]

  if (nrow(fitted_parameters) < 5) {
    return(empty_result)
  }

  c(
    spatial_summary(fitted_parameters[, 1]),
    spatial_summary(fitted_parameters[, 2]),
    spatial_summary(fitted_parameters[, 3])
  )
}
```

::: {.callout-caution title="Keep tryCatch, but test first"}
The full raster calculation needs `tryCatch()` so that a few failed resamples do not stop every cell.
Before running the map, use the one-cell code above without the outer spatial wrapper and inspect any errors.
:::

### Create spatial uncertainty layers

```{r}
#| label: spatial-uncertainty-layers
#| warning: false

spatial_uncertainty <- app(
  spatial_data,
  fit_PSO_uncertainty
)

names(spatial_uncertainty) <- c(
  "theta_d_median", "theta_d_lower", "theta_d_upper", "theta_d_width",
  "theta_w_median", "theta_w_lower", "theta_w_upper", "theta_w_width",
  "EF_max_median", "EF_max_lower", "EF_max_upper", "EF_max_width"
)
```

::: {.callout-note title="Start small while learning"}
Twenty resamples keep the course example manageable.
A research analysis may use more resamples after the function has been checked carefully.
PSO uncertainty mapping can take several minutes because every cell is fitted repeatedly.
:::

### Plot median parameters and uncertainty widths

```{r}
#| label: spatial-map-context

states <- project(vect(spData::us_states), crs(SM))

add_states <- function() {
  plot(states, add = TRUE, border = "grey20", lwd = 0.8)
}
```

```{r}
#| label: median-parameter-maps
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 11

median_maps <- spatial_uncertainty[[c(
  "theta_d_median",
  "theta_w_median",
  "EF_max_median"
)]]

plot(
  median_maps,
  main = c(
    expression("Median"~theta[d]),
    expression("Median"~theta[w]),
    expression("Median"~EF[max])
  ),
  fun = add_states,
  nc = 1
)
```

```{r}
#| label: uncertainty-width-maps
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 11

width_maps <- spatial_uncertainty[[c(
  "theta_d_width",
  "theta_w_width",
  "EF_max_width"
)]]

plot(
  width_maps,
  main = c(
    expression("95% ensemble width for"~theta[d]),
    expression("95% ensemble width for"~theta[w]),
    expression("95% ensemble width for"~EF[max])
  ),
  fun = add_states,
  nc = 1
)
```

The lower and upper layers remain available when you want to map the two ends of each parameter range directly.
Large width values identify locations where the parameter is especially sensitive to the selected observations.

## What should we conclude?

1. A single train/test split introduces the idea of out-of-sample prediction.
2. K-fold cross-validation rotates the validation group so every event is tested.
3. Repeated cross-validation creates an ensemble of parameter sets, predictions, and validation statistics.
4. Parameter ranges describe sensitivity of the fitted physical thresholds to resampling.
5. Prediction ribbons show variation among fitted ensemble members.
6. Spatial uncertainty maps distinguish locations with stable estimates from locations whose fitted parameters change strongly across resamples.
7. These ensemble ranges are useful diagnostic summaries, not complete confidence intervals.

## Let's discuss

1. Why should complete drydown events remain together in one fold?
2. How can a model have small training error but large validation error?
3. What does a wide parameter range tell us about the data at a site or raster cell?
4. Why is a narrow range suspicious when many parameter estimates reach an optimization bound?
5. Why can Random Forest have prediction uncertainty but not uncertainty in $\theta_d$ or $\theta_w$?
6. What additional sources of uncertainty are not represented by these resampling ranges?
